Consider the system of ordinary differential equations
[MATH: \mathbf{x}'(t) =
A
\mathbf{x}(t) +
\mathbf{f}(t)]
where [MATH: A] is a constant square matrix and [MATH: \mathbf{f}(t)] is a forcing vector.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll derive the formula for the particular solution of the above system using the method of variation of parameters.

Content:
Recall that the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous system is given by
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_c(t) = \Phi \, \mathbf{c}]
where [MATH: \mathbf{c}] is a vector of constants, and [MATH: \Phi] is the fundamental matrix.

Content:
As usual, for the method of variation of parameters, we'll look for a particular solution of our inhomogeneous system by varying the constant parameters, i.e., in the form
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)]
where [MATH: \mathbf{u}(t)] is a column vector of functions to be determined.

Content:
Differentiating [MATH: \mathbf{x}_p(t)] with respect to [MATH: t,] we get
[MATH: x_{p}^{′}(t)|= (Φu(t))^{′}; = Φu^{′}(t) + Φ^{′}u(t).]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: \mathbf{x}_p(t)] is a solution, substituting it back into the initial system gives a true equation:
[MATH: x^{′}(t)|= Ax(t) + f(t); Φu^{′}(t) + Φ^{′}u(t)|= AΦu(t) + f(t)]

Content:
Next, since [MATH: \Phi] is a fundamental matrix, [MATH: \Phi' = A \Phi.] Substituting this into the equation simplifies it to the following:
[MATH: Φu^{′}(t) + AΦu(t)|= AΦu(t) + f(t); Φu^{′}(t)|= f(t)]

Content:
Then, since [MATH: \Phi] is invertible, we can pre-multiply both sides by [MATH: \Phi^{-1}{:}]
[MATH: Φ^{− 1} ⋅ Φu^{′}(t)|= Φ^{− 1} ⋅ f(t); u^{′}(t)|= Φ^{− 1}(t)f(t)]

Content:
Finally, we integrate both sides of the final equations (ignoring the constant term):
[MATH: ∫u^{′}(t)dt|= ∫Φ^{− 1}f(t)dt; u(t)|= ∫Φ^{− 1}f(t)dt]

Content:
Therefore, our particular solution is
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Phi \displaystyle\int \Phi^{-1}\mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.]
